rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four usable editorial doors, not just four ways to say launch. "Bumble's AI writes the opening message on the app built around who sends it" is the cleanest story in the pile: tension, beat, timing, proof. B is competent, but "What happens when Bumble's AI writes your opening line" slides into product-review filler, and "Bumble sells subscriptions" smuggles in a fact the update did not give it.
gaps_in_A: "Dating apps are selling AI to users who say AI ruins dating" overreaches from one company plus "some users" into a category claim. A admits the proof gap, but the headline is still doing more than the facts support.
"the first substantive product move since the founder's return this year" is not explicitly in the update. It may be true, but it needs confirmation before it goes near a reporter.
The recommended next step, "newsjack-detector," is less immediately useful than fit-checking the strongest owned angle. The founder/interview path is the fastest route to real coverage.
gaps_in_B: "Bumble sells subscriptions" is not in the supplied update. Paying users does not give you permission to invent the revenue model.
"the market is trading on the launch" is an unsupported markets claim. The update says the stock fell and results are not reported; it does not say how investors are pricing the relaunch.
"What happens when Bumble's AI writes your opening line" is padded overlap with the women-message-first angle. Product testing is a format, not a strong separate strategic angle here.
"defensive-comment" mislabels the women-message-first story. This is product-values conflict, not a reactive statement posture.
